summary.text: Seafloor spreading is the process at mid-ocean ridges where volcanic activity makes new ocean crust, which then slowly moves away from the ridge.
In the 1960s Hess of Princeton and Robert Dietz proposed that the seafloor itself moves and carries the continents with it, an idea now known as plate tectonics.
Rocks get older with distance from a ridge, and magnetic stripes on one side mirror those on the other, recording past reversals of Earth's field.

facts.label: Fast ridges
facts.value: Open more than 90 mm per year

facts.label: Slow ridges
facts.value: Open less than 40 mm per year

facts.label: Highest known rate
facts.value: Over 200 mm/yr, East Pacific Rise, Miocene

items.prompt: What mainly drives the plates apart at a spreading ridge?

options.label: Magma pressure pushing up from below
Plates pulled by edges sinking far away
Tides raised by the Moon's pull
The spin of Earth flinging them outward

items.explain: The motivating force is slab pull at subduction zones rather than magma pressure, even though ridges typically have plenty of magma activity.

items.prompt: A ship drills seafloor rock at points farther and farther from a mid-ocean ridge. How do the rock ages change?
items.explain: New seabed forms at the spreading center and moves away, so older rocks lie farther from the spreading zone.

items.prompt: An ocean basin widens by 60 mm each year. How much new lithosphere does each plate on either side of the ridge gain per year?
items.explain: Each plate gains the spreading half-rate, which equals half of the total spreading rate.

items.prompt: Why should the magnetic stripes on one side of a mid-ocean ridge be a mirror image of those on the other?

options.label: Each side cooled under a different magnetic pole
Currents sweep magnetic grains into both sides
New crust forms at the center and moves both ways
Ships tow their sensors along the same track

items.explain: New crust forms at the ridge and moves away on both sides, so each band of past magnetic polarity is carried off in both directions.

items.prompt: Heat builds up beneath the base of a continent's crust. What happens to the land above as a result?
items.explain: Heated crust becomes less dense and rises into a broad dome, and as it bows upward fractures form that grow into rifts.

items.prompt: A young sea in a new rift dries out partly or fully several times before it settles. What does this leave behind in the rift valley?
items.explain: Each round of evaporation of the new sea leaves large evaporite deposits in the rift valley.
